paragraphs.en: The Stanford marshmallow ( (棉花糖) ) test was {originally} conducted by psychologist Walter Mischel in the late 1960s.This experiment has {forever} changed our understanding of self-control and delayed gratification.Children aged four to six at a {nursery} school were placed in a room.A single {sugary} treat was placed on a table.Each child was told if they waited for 15 minutes before eating the treat, they would be given a second treat.The researcher {delivered} this message and then {exited} , leaving the children alone in the room.Some children {folded} immediately under pressure, while others showed {resistance} to the temptation.Years later, when researchers {inquired} about the participants' life outcomes, there was a connection between the ability to {postpone} gratification and various forms of success.
paragraphs.cn: 斯坦福棉花糖实验 <u> 最初 </u> 是由心理学家沃尔特·米谢尔在20世纪60年代末进行的。这个实验 <u> 永远 </u> 改变了我们对自我控制和延迟满足的认识。在一所 <u> 幼儿园 </u> 里，年龄在4岁到6岁的孩子被安排在一个房间里。桌上放着一块 <u> 甜甜的 </u> 糖果。每个孩子都被告知，如果他们在吃这块糖果之前等待15分钟，就会得到第二块糖果。研究人员 <u> 传达 </u> 完信息后就 <u> 离开 </u> 了，把孩子们单独留在房间里。一些孩子在压力之下马上就 <u> 妥协 </u> 了，而另一些孩子则对诱惑表现出了 <u> 抵抗力 </u> 。多年后，当研究人员 <u> 询问 </u> 参与者的人生成就时发现， <u> 延迟 </u> 满足的能力与各种形式的成功之间存在着某种联系。

paragraphs.en: As adults, we face a {version} of the marshmallow test every day.We're not tempted ( (诱惑) ) by sugary treats, but by our computers, phones, and {tablets} —all the devices that connect us to the global {delivery} system for various types of information that do to us what marshmallows do to {preschoolers} .We often find ourselves {wrestling} with distractions.
paragraphs.cn: 作为成年人，我们每天都要面对另一种 <u> 形式 </u> 的棉花糖实验。诱惑我们的并非甜甜的糖果，而是电脑、手机和 <u> 平板电脑 </u> ——所有这些将我们与各类信息的全球 <u> 传递 </u> 系统相连接的设备，这些信息对我们造成的影响就像棉花糖对 <u> 学龄前儿童 </u> 的影响一样。我们经常发现自己在与分散注意力的事物相 <u> 抗争 </u> 。

paragraphs.en: We are tempted by sugary treats.One reason is that sweet {flavors} often indicated ripe fruits like {apples} or {grapes} that were safe to eat, while bitter tastes could signal {poison} .It is not just about safety.Our {ancestors} lived in a calorie-poor world. {Fats} and sugars were both crucial for survival, but the latter offered a quick source of energy, which could have distinguished between survival and {death} .Therefore, our brains developed a response {mechanism} to sugary treats that reflected their value—a feeling of reward and satisfaction.But as we've {reshaped} the world around us, sugary {desserts} and {delicious} treats became readily available, and we no longer needed to hunt {lambs} , which {dramatically} reduced the {cost} and effort {involved} in obtaining calories.Yet we still have the same brains we had {thousands} of years ago, and this {mismatch} is at the heart of why so many of us struggle to {resist} {tempting} foods that we know we shouldn't eat.
paragraphs.cn: 我们会受到甜食的诱惑。其中一个原因在于，甜 <u> 味 </u> 通常暗示了 <u> 苹果 </u> 、 <u> 葡萄 </u> 等可以安全食用的成熟水果，而苦味则可能是有 <u> 毒 </u> 的标志。这不仅仅是安全的问题。我们的 <u> 祖先 </u> 生活在一个热量匮乏的世界。 <u> 脂肪 </u> 和糖对于生存而言都是至关重要的，但后者能迅速提供能量，它在当时可能决定了生 <u> 死 </u> 存 <u> 亡 </u> 。因此，我们的大脑对甜食形成了一种反应 <u> 机制 </u> ，这种机制反映了甜食的价值——一种受到奖赏的、满足的感受。但是，随着我们对周遭世界的 <u> 改造 </u> ，含糖的 <u> 甜点 </u> 和 <u> 美味的 </u> 食品变得唾手可得，我们也不再需要捕猎 <u> 羔羊 </u> ，这 <u> 大大 </u> 降低了获取热量所 <u> 涉及的成本 </u> 和精力。然而，我们的大脑仍然和 <u> 几千 </u> 年前一样，而这种 <u> 不匹配 </u> 正是我们当中这么多人难以 <u> 抵抗 </u> 那些我们明知不该吃的、 <u> 诱人的 </u> 食物的核心原因。

paragraphs.en: A similar process is at work in our response to information.Our {formative} {environment} as a {species} was information-poor, so our brains developed a mechanism that {prized} new information.But global {connectivity} has greatly changed our information environment.We are now {ceaselessly} bombarded ( (轰炸) ) with new information.With a simple click on the {keyboard} , we can {download} an overwhelming amount of data.We {surf} the internet, {subscribe} to countless newsletters, and our inboxes fill up with {mail} , making it increasingly difficult to {guard} our attention.The digital cloud is not just a place where data is stored; it has made our minds {cloudy} , too.Therefore, just as we need to be more {thoughtful} about our {caloric} {consumption} , we must learn to {swim} through the ocean of information without sinking into a {soup} of meaningless data, resisting the {temptation} of the mental“ {junk} food” in order to manage our time most {effectively} .
paragraphs.cn: 类似的过程也在我们对信息的反应中发挥作用。作为一个 <u> 物种 </u> ，我们 <u> 形成 </u> 期所处的 <u> 环境 </u> 是信息匮乏的，因此我们的大脑形成了一种 <u> 重视 </u> 新信息的机制。但全球的 <u> 互联互通 </u> 极大地改变了我们的信息环境。现在，我们 <u> 不停地 </u> 受到新信息的轰炸。只需简单地敲击一下 <u> 键盘 </u> ，我们就能 <u> 下载 </u> 大量的数据。我们在互联网上 <u> 冲浪 </u> ， <u> 订阅 </u> 无数的时事通讯，收件箱被 <u> 邮件 </u> 塞得满满的，这使得我们越来越难以 <u> 维系 </u> 我们的注意力。数字“云”不仅是一个存储数据的地方，还让我们的头脑也变得“ <u> 云里雾里 </u> ”。因此，正如我们需要对 <u> 热量的摄入 </u> 多加 <u> 思考 </u> 一样，我们必须学会在信息的海洋中畅 <u> 游 </u> ，而不会沉没在毫无意义的数据 <u> 洪流 </u> 中，我们要抵制精神上的“ <u> 垃圾 </u> 食品”的 <u> 诱惑 </u> ，以便最 <u> 有效地 </u> 管理我们的时间。 5NoOncib/NjiX02BpMIzP4m+378Hw1xTRxUdPaP/PFjKUFq4K2G7tp6ZLYoCE601yW1W39VMdLmovFdSHs4nVQ==
